title: E-Discovery and Large-Scale Document Analysis
answer: Predictive coding, cross-lingual review, audio and video evidence, privilege logging, and sentiment analysis of corporate messaging.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review
children.blurb: Predictive coding and technology-assisted review, often called TAR, are methods for finding relevant documents in large e-discovery collections by using machine learning to rank or classify documents.

children.name: Cross-Lingual Discovery
children.blurb: Cross-lingual discovery is the process of locating, assessing, and producing documents written in languages other than the primary language of a legal matter.

children.name: Audio and Video Evidence
children.blurb: Audio and video evidence in e-discovery covers recorded calls, voicemail, body camera footage, surveillance video, meeting recordings, and multimedia attachments in email or chat.

children.name: Automated Privilege Logging
children.blurb: Automated privilege logging covers the identification and description of documents withheld from production in e-discovery on grounds such as attorney-client privilege or work product protection.

children.name: Intent and Sentiment in Corporate Communications
children.blurb: This topic covers the use of language analysis to infer what a communicator intended and how they felt in corporate records such as email, chat, memos, board minutes, and earnings call transcripts.

sections.body: E-discovery and large-scale document analysis is the use of AI to find, sort, and review the electronic records that parties exchange in litigation and investigations. In practice, systems score documents for relevance, group near duplicates, translate foreign-language material, transcribe audio and video, and flag messages that may be privileged. Predictive coding and technology-assisted review let a human reviewer train a model on a small set of coded documents, then apply that model to millions of others. Cross-lingual discovery extends the same review to multilingual collections without waiting for every document to be translated by hand. Audio and video evidence tools turn speech into searchable text and detect speakers or events. Automated privilege logging builds a record of what was withheld and why, while intent and sentiment analysis tries to read tone and purpose in corporate communications.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is mature in some narrow tasks and fragile in others. Relevance ranking and near-duplicate detection are widely used and can reduce review volume, but they still depend on good training data and careful quality control. Cross-lingual review works better for high-resource languages than for low-resource ones, and legal meaning can shift across jurisdictions. Audio and video analysis has improved with speech recognition, yet accents, poor recordings, and overlapping speakers remain hard. Privilege logging is partly automated, but privilege calls are legal judgments, so a human must still make the final call. Sentiment and intent models can surface patterns in corporate messaging, but they cannot reliably prove what a person meant, and the site tracks 29 AI case law precedents that show courts are still testing how much deference to give these tools.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages in this section divide the work by evidence type and by task. Predictive Coding and Technology-Assisted Review is the place to start for the core workflow of training a model and measuring its recall and precision. Cross-Lingual Discovery follows the same review logic into multilingual collections, where translation quality and language coverage decide what can be found. Audio and Video Evidence covers the shift from text to speech, including transcription, speaker identification, and the review of recorded meetings or calls. Automated Privilege Logging explains how systems draft and check logs, and why human legal review remains central. Intent and Sentiment in Corporate Communications looks at tone, purpose, and patterns in messages, a task that is often more interpretive than predictive, and together these pages show how a large document set is reduced to a reviewable record.
